docs/architecture.html.title: Architecture | Invex.StructuredText
docs/architecture.html.summary: Architecture This page explains how the three packages fit together and the design decisions behind them. Useful if you want to extend the library, contribute, or build your own generator on top of the core. Package layering ┌─────────────────────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Invex.StructuredText │ │ Invex.StructuredText │ │ .GithubActions │ │ .AzureDevopsPipelines │ │ │ │ │ │ • GithubActionWriter │ │ • DevopsPipelineWriter │ │ • DependabotConfigWriter │ │ • DevopsExpressionPrinter │ │ • GithubExpressionPrinter │ │ • Tex.DevOps (DevopsContexts) │ │ • Tex.GitHub (GitHubContexts) │ │ • DevopsRuntimeExpr │ │ • GithubActionModel/* │ │ • DevopsPipelineModel/* │ │ • DependabotConfigModel/* │ │ │ └───────────────┬─────────────────┘ └──────────────────┬───────────────────┘ │ │ └───────────────────┬───────────────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Invex.StructuredText (core) │ │ │ │ • StructuredTextWriter │ │ • Tex (the expression entry point) │ │ • Expr, BoolExpr, StringExpr, … │ │ • Template │ │ • ExpressionPrinter (base) │ └─────────────────────────────────────┘ Core (Invex.StructuredText) StructuredTextWriter A minimal, indentation-aware text writer. WriteSection returns an IDisposable scope that decrements the indent on dispose, so the structure of the generating C# code mirrors the structure of the generated YAML. A version counter makes stale scopes harmless after Reset(). See StructuredTextWriter. The expression tree Expr is an abstract record with four typed roots: BoolExpr, StringExpr, NumberExpr and JsonExpr. The result type decides which operations the compiler offers, so If = Tex.GitHub.Ref (a string) does not compile. The concrete nodes are grouped by concern: Literals: StringLiteral, NumberLiteral, BoolLiteral, NullLiteral, created implicitly from C# literals Context paths: StringContext, BoolContext, NumberContext, JsonContext, used by the generated catalogues such as Tex.GitHub Access and casts: MemberAccessExpr, IndexAccessExpr, StringCast, BoolCast, NumberCast Logic: ComparisonExpr, LogicalExpr (flattened, so a && b && c is one node), NotExpr Functions: BoolFunction, StringFunction, JsonFunction, named with the constants in FunctionNames References: SecretRef, VariableRef, InputRef, MatrixRef, StepOutputRef, JobOutputRef, JobResultRef and ResultLiteral, which each platform spells its own way Raw text: RawExpr and its typed siblings, for the Tex.Raw escape hatch Because they are records, expressions compare structurally, and DescendantsAndSelf() walks the tree. Atom uses that to find the jobs a condition depends on. Tex is the single entry point that creates them. Platform packages and libraries add members to it with C# 14 extension(Tex) blocks, which is how Tex.GitHub, Tex.DevOps and Atom's Tex.ParamOutput appear on the same type. Template Template is a sequence of literal text and embedded expressions. It is an interpolated string handler, so $"v{Tex.GitHub.RunNumber}" builds one directly, and it converts implicitly from string, Expr, bool and numbers. Every model property that can hold an expression, other than conditions, is a Template. ExpressionPrinter The abstract printer renders an Expr (Print) or a Template (Render). The base class handles operator precedence (adding parentheses only where needed), literal quoting and escaping, member and index access, casts and raw text. A platform printer supplies what differs: WrapEmbedded: the delimiters around an expression inside a template, such as ${{ … }}. PrintReference and PrintResult: how references and job results are spelled. Optional overrides: FunctionName, PrintComparison, PrintLogical, PrintNot, RenderEmbedded and others. Azure DevOps overrides the logic members to print and(…), eq(…), and RenderEmbedded to choose between $(…), ${{ … }} and $[ … ]. A node a printer can't express throws NotSupportedException rather than producing invalid YAML. Platform packages Each platform package contains: Model types — records that mirror the official YAML schema for the platform. Conditions are BoolExpr, and almost every other scalar property is a Template, so any value can contain expressions. A writer — walks the model and emits YAML through a StructuredTextWriter, calling the platform expression printer for every expression-valued property. An expression printer — GithubExpressionPrinter or DevopsExpressionPrinter, an ExpressionPrinter for the platform's syntax. A context catalogue — Tex.GitHub or Tex.DevOps. The GitHub catalogue is generated at build time from Contexts/github.contexts by Invex.StructuredText.Generators. GitHub Actions (Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions) GithubActionWriter — serializes a GithubAction model to workflow YAML. DependabotConfigWriter — serializes a DependabotConfig model to dependabot.yml. GithubExpressionPrinter — prints expressions using GitHub's syntax, and ${{ }} inside templates. Model types — strongly-typed records for all GitHub Actions concepts (triggers, jobs, steps, matrix, permissions, etc.) in GithubActionModel, and for Dependabot in DependabotConfigModel.Model. Azure DevOps Pipelines (Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines) DevopsPipelineWriter — serializes a DevopsPipeline model to pipeline YAML. DevopsExpressionPrinter — prints expressions using Azure DevOps syntax. DevopsRuntimeExpr — created by Tex.DevOps.Runtime(…), embeds an expression as a $[ … ] runtime expression. Model types — strongly-typed records and unions for pipelines, stages, jobs, steps, resources, triggers, variables, deployment strategies, and more, under DevopsPipelineModel.*. Discriminated unions YAML schemas are full of "one of" shapes (a step is run: or uses:; a pool is a name or a spec). These are modeled as discriminated unions using the Dunet source generator: an abstract base record with nested variant records. You construct the variant you need (new Step.RunStep { ... }), and the writers pattern-match on the variant to emit the right YAML shape. This rules out invalid combinations at compile time. Schema fidelity The GitHub workflow JSON schema and Dependabot v2 JSON schema are checked into the source tree alongside the models, and the Azure DevOps models carry XML docs lifted from the official YAML schema reference. Property names map mechanically to YAML keys (PascalCase → kebab-case / camelCase as appropriate per platform). Public API discipline The libraries use: [PublicAPI] annotations (JetBrains.Annotations) on all public surface Public API surface snapshot tests (PublicApiSurfaceTests with verified .txt baselines in each test project), so any accidental API change shows up as a test diff Targets .NET 10 Extending the library Goal How New target platform Reference the core, define model records, write an ExpressionPrinter subclass and a writer over StructuredTextWriter New Tex member Add an extension(Tex) block in your package, returning existing node types where you can New context in the GitHub catalogue Add a line to Contexts/github.contexts; the generator adds the member and its XML docs Platform-specific expression syntax Follow the pattern of DevopsRuntimeExpr: define the record in the platform package and print it in that platform's printer (PrintOther or RenderEmbedded) See also StructuredTextWriter: the writer every generator is built on Expressions: writing your own printer FAQ: common questions about the model design StructuredTextWriter, Tex, Expr, ExpressionPrinter

docs/azure-devops-pipelines.html.title: Azure DevOps Pipelines | Invex.StructuredText
docs/azure-devops-pipelines.html.summary: Azure DevOps Pipelines The Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines package generates Azure Pipelines YAML from a strongly-typed model rooted at DevopsPipeline (namespace Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines.DevopsPipelineModel.*). Read this page when you generate Azure Pipelines: pipeline shapes, triggers, steps, pools, variables, deployment jobs, and Azure DevOps expression syntax. var writer = new DevopsPipelineWriter(); writer.Write(pipeline); var yaml = writer.TextWriter.ToString(); The four pipeline shapes Azure Pipelines YAML allows four top-level shapes, and DevopsPipeline is a union over exactly those four: Variant YAML shape DevopsPipelineWithSteps steps: at the root (implicit single job) DevopsPipelineWithJobs jobs: at the root (implicit single stage) DevopsPipelineWithStages stages: — the full multi-stage syntax DevopsPipelineWithExtends extends: — extend a pipeline template All four share the common pipeline-level properties: Name (run number format), Trigger, Pr, Schedules, Parameters, Pool, Variables, resources, LockBehavior, and AppendCommitMessageToRunName. Steps pipeline var pipeline = new DevopsPipeline.DevopsPipelineWithSteps { Pool = new Pool.PoolSpec { VmImage = "ubuntu-latest" }, Trigger = new Trigger.BranchList { Branches = ["main"] }, Steps = [ new Step.Script { ScriptContent = "echo hello" }, ], }; trigger: branches: include: [ main ] pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - script: echo hello Jobs pipeline var pipeline = new DevopsPipeline.DevopsPipelineWithJobs { Jobs = [ new Job.RegularJob { JobId = "build", DisplayName = "Build", Pool = new Pool.PoolSpec { VmImage = "ubuntu-latest" }, Steps = [ new Step.Script { ScriptContent = "dotnet build" }, ], }, new Job.RegularJob { JobId = "test", DependsOn = ["build"], Condition = Tex.Success(), Steps = [ new Step.Script { ScriptContent = "dotnet test" }, ], }, ], }; Stages pipeline var pipeline = new DevopsPipeline.DevopsPipelineWithStages { Stages = [ new Stage.StageDefinition { StageId = "Build", Jobs = [ /* Job.RegularJob ... */ ], }, new Stage.StageDefinition { StageId = "Deploy", DependsOn = ["Build"], Condition = Tex.Success(), Jobs = [ /* deployment jobs ... */ ], }, ], }; Extends pipeline var pipeline = new DevopsPipeline.DevopsPipelineWithExtends { Extends = new Extends { Template = "pipeline-template.yml@templates", Parameters = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["configuration"] = "Release", }, }, }; Triggers // CI trigger: branch list Trigger = new Trigger.BranchList { Branches = ["main", "release/*"] }, // CI trigger: full control Trigger = new Trigger.Full { Batch = true, Branches = new IncludeExcludeFilters { Include = ["main"], Exclude = ["experimental/*"], }, Paths = new IncludeExcludeFilters { Include = ["src/*"] }, }, // Disable CI triggers entirely Trigger = new Trigger.None(), Pr (pull-request triggers) and Schedules (cron triggers) follow the same pattern with their own union/record types. Steps Step is a union over the twelve Azure Pipelines step kinds: Variant YAML key Required property Task task: TaskName (+ Inputs) Script script: ScriptContent Bash bash: ScriptContent PowerShell powershell: ScriptContent Pwsh pwsh: ScriptContent Checkout checkout: Repository Download download: Pipeline DownloadBuild downloadBuild: Build GetPackage getPackage: Package Publish publish: PublishPath Template template: TemplatePath ReviewApp reviewApp: ReviewAppType All script/task-like steps share the common properties DisplayName, Name, Condition, ContinueOnError, Enabled, Env, Target, TimeoutInMinutes, and RetryCountOnTaskFailure. Steps = [ new Step.Checkout { Repository = "self", FetchDepth = 0, Lfs = true, }, new Step.Task { TaskName = "UseDotNet@2", DisplayName = "Install .NET SDK", Inputs = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["packageType"] = "sdk", ["version"] = "10.0.x", }, }, new Step.Script { ScriptContent = "dotnet build -c Release", DisplayName = "Build", Env = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["DOTNET_NOLOGO"] = "true", }, }, new Step.Publish { PublishPath = Tex.DevOps.Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory, Artifact = "drop", Condition = Tex.Always(), }, ], Pools // Microsoft-hosted image Pool = new Pool.PoolSpec { VmImage = "ubuntu-latest" }, // Named (self-hosted) pool Pool = new Pool.PoolName { Name = "Default" }, Variables Variables is a union supporting both YAML syntaxes: // Mapping syntax: name/value pairs Variables = new Variables.Dictionary { Values = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["buildConfiguration"] = "Release", }, }, // List syntax: named variables, groups, and templates Variables = new Variables.VariableList { Values = [ new Variable.Name { VariableName = "buildConfiguration", Value = "Release", ReadOnly = true, }, new Variable.Group { GroupName = "shared-secrets" }, new Variable.Template { TemplatePath = "variables/common.yml" }, ], }, Reference variables in steps with Tex.Variable, which is written in macro syntax: new Step.Script { ScriptContent = $"dotnet build -c {Tex.Variable("buildConfiguration")}", // dotnet build -c $(buildConfiguration) } Deployment jobs and strategies Deployment jobs (Job.Deployment) target an environment and require a DeploymentStrategy — a union over RunOnce, Rolling, and Canary, each with lifecycle hooks (PreDeploy, Deploy, RouteTraffic, PostRouteTraffic, OnSuccess, OnFailure): new Job.Deployment { DeploymentId = "deploy_prod", DisplayName = "Deploy to production", Environment = new DeploymentEnvironment.EnvironmentName { Name = "production", }, Strategy = new DeploymentStrategy.RunOnce { Deploy = new DeploymentHook { Steps = [ new Step.Script { ScriptContent = "./deploy.sh" }, ], }, OnFailure = new DeploymentHook { Steps = [ new Step.Script { ScriptContent = "./rollback.sh" }, ], }, }, } Rolling deployments add MaxParallel; canary deployments require Increments (e.g. [10, 20, 70]). Resources PipelineResources / Resources lets you declare repositories, pipelines, builds, containers, packages, and webhooks used by the pipeline — each modeled with its own strongly-typed record under DevopsPipelineModel.Resources. Templates and parameters Job, stage, step, and variable lists each have a Template variant for referencing template files with Parameters. Pipeline-level Parameters define runtime parameters for the pipeline (or template parameters when authoring templates). Expressions in Azure DevOps Azure DevOps uses the same expression API as GitHub Actions (see Expressions), printed with DevopsExpressionPrinter. Conditions use the function-style syntax: C# Output a && b and(a, b) a \|\| b or(a, b) !a not(a) a.Eq("x"), a.Ne("x") eq(a, 'x'), ne(a, 'x') n.Lt(1), n.Le(1), n.Gt(1), n.Ge(1) lt(n, 1), le(n, 1), gt(n, 1), ge(n, 1) a.Contains("x") contains(a, 'x') Tex.Success(), Tex.Failure(), Tex.Cancelled(), Tex.Always() succeeded(), failed(), canceled(), always() Tex.JobResult("build").Eq(Tex.Result(RunResult.Success)) eq(dependencies.build.result, 'Succeeded') Condition = Tex.DevOps.Build.SourceBranch.Eq("refs/heads/main") && !Tex.DevOps.Build.Reason.Eq("PullRequest"), // condition: and(eq(variables['Build.SourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/main'), not(eq(variables['Build.Reason'], 'PullRequest'))) Inside a template, each kind of value is embedded with the syntax Azure DevOps expects for it: C# Embedded as Tex.Variable("x"), Tex.Secret("x"), Tex.Matrix("x") $(x) (macro) Tex.StepOutput("step", "out") $(step.out) (macro) Tex.Input("x") ${{ parameters.x }} (template expression) Tex.JobOutput("job", "out", "step") $[ dependencies.job.outputs['step.out'] ] (runtime expression) Tex.DevOps.Runtime(expression) $[ expression ] (runtime expression) Any expression that reads a job output or job result $[ expression ] (runtime expression) Any other expression ${{ expression }} (template expression) Important The printer throws NotSupportedException for combinations Azure DevOps can't evaluate, rather than writing YAML that silently misbehaves: A runtime expression combined with text, such as $"v{Tex.JobOutput("Setup", "version", "Info")}". Azure DevOps only evaluates $[ … ] when it is the whole value. An input (Tex.Input) in a condition or a runtime expression. Parameters only exist at compile time. A secret, matrix value or step output inside a compound expression such as Tex.Format(...), which would be a compile-time ${{ … }}. Interpolate them directly as macros, or wrap the expression in Tex.DevOps.Runtime. In each case, bind the value to a variable and use Tex.Variable("name"). Tex.DevOps lists the common predefined variables, such as Tex.DevOps.Build.SourceBranch, Tex.DevOps.Build.BuildId, Tex.DevOps.System.AccessToken, Tex.DevOps.Agent.Os and Tex.DevOps.PipelineWorkspace. Use Tex.Variable("Name") for any other variable. Variables = new Variables.Dictionary { Values = new Dictionary<string, Template> { // isMain: $[ eq(variables['Build.SourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/main') ] ["isMain"] = Tex.DevOps.Runtime(Tex.DevOps.Build.SourceBranch.Eq("refs/heads/main")), }, }, Note Azure DevOps has no fromJSON, so Tex.FromJson throws NotSupportedException here. ToJson() prints convertToJson(...), Join puts the separator first (join(',', items)), and array membership (value.In(items), items.Contains(value)) prints containsValue(items, value). See also Getting Started: your first pipeline Expressions: the expression API shared with GitHub Actions The model closely follows the Azure Pipelines YAML schema — property names and XML docs mirror the official documentation. DevopsPipeline, DevopsPipelineWriter, DevopsExpressionPrinter

docs/dependabot.html.title: Dependabot Configuration | Invex.StructuredText
docs/dependabot.html.summary: Dependabot Configuration The Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions package also generates Dependabot v2 configuration files from the DependabotConfig model (namespace Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions.DependabotConfigModel.Model). Use it when you want dependabot.yml generated alongside your workflows, with the same type checking. var writer = new DependabotConfigWriter(); writer.WriteConfig(config); var yaml = writer.TextWriter.ToString(); Minimal config var config = new DependabotConfig { Updates = [ new DependabotUpdate { PackageEcosystem = "nuget", Directory = "/", Schedule = new() { Interval = ScheduleInterval.Weekly }, }, ], }; version: 2 updates: - package-ecosystem: nuget directory: / schedule: interval: weekly PackageEcosystem takes the package-ecosystem YAML value as a string. To pick it from the PackageEcosystem enum instead, use the ToYamlValue() extension method: new DependabotUpdate { PackageEcosystem = PackageEcosystem.GithubActions.ToYamlValue(), // "github-actions" Directory = "/", Schedule = new() { Interval = ScheduleInterval.Weekly }, } Version defaults to 2 (the only valid value), so you never need to set it. The model at a glance DependabotConfig ├── Version (= 2) ├── EnableBetaEcosystems ├── Registries (name → DependabotRegistry) ├── MultiEcosystemGroups (name → DependabotMultiEcosystemGroup) └── Updates (list of DependabotUpdate) ├── PackageEcosystem, Directory / Directories, TargetBranch ├── Schedule (interval, day, time, timezone, cronjob) ├── Allow, Ignore, ExcludePaths ├── Groups (name → DependabotGroup) ├── Registries, Labels, Assignees, Milestone ├── CommitMessage, PullRequestBranchName, RebaseStrategy ├── OpenPullRequestsLimit, Cooldown, Vendor ├── VersioningStrategy, InsecureExternalCodeExecution └── MultiEcosystemGroup, Patterns Private registries var config = new DependabotConfig { Registries = new Dictionary<string, DependabotRegistry> { ["my-nuget"] = new() { Type = RegistryType.NugetFeed, Url = "https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/myorg/_packaging/my-feed/nuget/v3/index.json", Token = "${{ secrets.FEED_TOKEN }}", }, ["dockerhub"] = new() { Type = RegistryType.DockerRegistry, Url = "https://registry.hub.docker.com", Username = "my-user", Password = "${{ secrets.DOCKER_TOKEN }}", ReplacesBase = true, }, }, Updates = [ new DependabotUpdate { PackageEcosystem = "nuget", Directory = "/", Schedule = new() { Interval = ScheduleInterval.Daily }, Registries = new DependabotRegistries.Named("my-nuget"), }, ], }; Note Dependabot config values are plain strings — ${{ secrets.* }} references are passed through verbatim, exactly as Dependabot expects. Schedules Schedule = new DependabotSchedule { Interval = ScheduleInterval.Weekly, // Daily | Weekly | Monthly | Quarterly | Semiannually | Yearly | Cron Day = ScheduleDay.Monday, Time = "06:00", Timezone = "Europe/London", }, // or cron-based: Schedule = new DependabotSchedule { Interval = ScheduleInterval.Cron, Cronjob = "0 6 * * 1", }, Groups Group related dependencies into a single pull request: Groups = new Dictionary<string, DependabotGroup> { ["test-packages"] = new DependabotGroup.FromPatterns { Patterns = ["NUnit*", "Shouldly", "Verify*"], }, ["analyzers"] = new DependabotGroup.FromPatterns { Patterns = ["*.Analyzers"], }, }, Use new DependabotRegistries.All() to opt an update into every configured registry, or new DependabotRegistries.Named(...) for a specific list. Group variants include FromPatterns, FromExcludePatterns, FromType, FromUpdateTypes, and FromGroupBy. Multi-ecosystem groups consolidate PRs across package managers — define them at the config level via MultiEcosystemGroups and reference them per-update via MultiEcosystemGroup and Patterns. Allow / ignore rules Allow = [ new DependabotAllow { DependencyName = "Microsoft.*", DependencyType = DependencyType.Production, }, ], Ignore = [ new DependabotIgnore { DependencyName = "Newtonsoft.Json", UpdateTypes = [SemverUpdateType.VersionUpdateSemverMajor], Versions = new DependabotVersions.Multiple(["13.x"]), }, ], Pull-request presentation CommitMessage = new DependabotCommitMessage { Prefix = "deps", PrefixDevelopment = null, Include = CommitMessageInclude.Scope, }, Labels = ["dependencies"], Assignees = ["octocat"], OpenPullRequestsLimit = 10, See also GitHub Actions Workflows — workflow generation from the same package The model closely mirrors the official dependabot-2.0 JSON schema; the schema file is included in the source tree for reference. DependabotConfig, DependabotConfigWriter

docs/expressions.html.title: Expressions | Invex.StructuredText
docs/expressions.html.summary: Expressions The expression API (namespace Invex.StructuredText.Expressions) lets you write conditions, references and interpolated values in C# instead of hand-writing ${{ … }} or $( … ) strings. You build a small typed tree, and the platform writer prints it in that platform's syntax. Read this page whenever a value in your model is a condition, a reference to a secret or another job's output, or text built from other values. using Invex.StructuredText.Expressions; using Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions; BoolExpr publish = Tex.GitHub.EventName.Eq("push") && !Tex.GitHub.Ref.StartsWith("refs/tags/"); // if: github.event_name == 'push' && !startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/') Start with Tex Everything that creates an expression from scratch is a member of the static class Tex. Type Tex. and IntelliSense lists all of it: Group Members References Secret(name), Variable(name), Input(name), Matrix(name), StepOutput(step, output), JobOutput(job, output, step?), JobResult(job), Result(RunResult) Status checks Success(), Always(), Failure(), Cancelled() Functions All(conditions), Any(conditions), Format(format, args), HashFiles(patterns), FromJson(json), Null, Join(separator, templates) Escape hatch Raw(text) Platform contexts Tex.GitHub (from Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions), Tex.DevOps (from Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines) Tex.GitHub and Tex.DevOps are C# 14 extension members, so they appear once you reference the platform package and import its namespace. Libraries built on top can add their own the same way (Atom adds Tex.ParamOutput). Once you have an expression, its own members do the rest: Eq, Contains, StartsWith, the &&, || and ! operators, and indexers on JSON values. Tip Add using static Invex.StructuredText.Expressions.Tex; to drop the prefix and write Secret("TOKEN"), Success() or GitHub.Ref. Expression types Each expression has a result type, and the compiler only offers the operations that make sense for it: Type What it is Operations BoolExpr A condition &&, \|\|, !, Eq, Ne StringExpr A string value Eq, Ne, Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith, In(collection) NumberExpr A number Eq, Ne, Lt, Le, Gt, Ge JsonExpr An object or array ["name"], [index], AsString(), AsBool(), AsNumber(), Contains(element), Join, ToJson All four derive from Expr. C# literals convert implicitly: "push" becomes a quoted string literal, 100 a number literal and true a boolean literal, so Tex.GitHub.EventName.Eq("push") prints github.event_name == 'push'. Quotes inside literals are escaped for you. Conditions Conditions are BoolExpr values combined with the C# operators. Parentheses are added only where precedence needs them, and the platform decides the spelling: var isPush = Tex.GitHub.EventName.Eq("push"); var onMain = Tex.GitHub.Ref.Eq("refs/heads/main"); var isTag = Tex.GitHub.Ref.StartsWith("refs/tags/"); var isBot = Tex.GitHub.Actor.Eq("dependabot[bot]"); If = isPush && onMain, // github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' If = (isPush || isTag) && !isBot, // (github.event_name == 'push' || startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/')) && !(github.actor == 'dependabot[bot]') If = Tex.All([isPush, onMain, Tex.Success()]), // github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && success() If = Tex.Always() && Tex.JobResult("test").Eq(Tex.Result(RunResult.Failure)), // always() && needs.test.result == 'failure' Model properties that hold a condition (If on GitHub jobs and steps, Condition in Azure DevOps) are typed BoolExpr, so anything else is a compile error. Tex.All and Tex.Any take any number of conditions, which is handy when you build them in a loop. Values and templates Every other expression-capable property (names, run lines, env values, with inputs, outputs) is a Template. A Template is literal text with expressions embedded in it, and you create one with an ordinary string or an interpolated string: Name = "Build", // Build Env = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["NUGET_API_KEY"] = Tex.Secret("NUGET_API_KEY"), // ${{ secrets.NUGET_API_KEY }} }, Run = [$"dotnet build -p:Version=1.0.{Tex.GitHub.RunNumber}"], // dotnet build -p:Version=1.0.${{ github.run_number }} Group = $"{Tex.GitHub.Workflow}-{Tex.GitHub.Ref}", // ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }} Plain strings stay literal text, and expressions in the holes are wrapped in the platform's delimiters. Holes that are plain C# values (strings, numbers, bool) are written as text. Tex.Join joins several templates with a separator: Tex.Join("-", ["build", Tex.Matrix("os"), Tex.Matrix("framework")]) // build-${{ matrix.os }}-${{ matrix.framework }} Warning A conditional that mixes an interpolated string with a plain string needs a (Template) cast on the interpolated branch: Name = isNightly ? (Template)$"Nightly {Tex.GitHub.RunNumber}" : "Release". Without it, C# builds a string for the ternary and the expression is written as plain text (Nightly github.run_number) instead of Nightly ${{ github.run_number }}. References C# GitHub Actions Azure DevOps Tex.Secret("TOKEN") secrets.TOKEN $(TOKEN) Tex.Variable("REGION") vars.REGION $(REGION) Tex.Input("dry-run") inputs.dry-run ${{ parameters['dry-run'] }} Tex.Matrix("os") matrix.os $(os) Tex.StepOutput("version", "semver") steps.version.outputs.semver $(version.semver) Tex.JobOutput("setup", "version", "step") needs.setup.outputs.version $[ dependencies.setup.outputs['step.version'] ] Tex.JobResult("test") needs.test.result dependencies.test.result Tex.Result(RunResult.Failure) 'failure' 'Failed' The GitHub column shows the bare expression; inside a template it is wrapped in ${{ }}. The Azure DevOps column shows how each reference is embedded in a template, because Azure DevOps has a different syntax for each kind of value. The step argument of JobOutput is only used by Azure DevOps, where job outputs are addressed through the step that set them. Platform contexts Tex.GitHub is a catalogue of the GitHub Actions contexts, generated from the documented context list with XML docs on every member: Tex.GitHub.Ref // github.ref (StringExpr) Tex.GitHub.Event.PullRequest.Number // github.event.pull_request.number (NumberExpr) Tex.GitHub.Event.PullRequest.Draft // github.event.pull_request.draft (BoolExpr) Tex.GitHub.Runner.Os // runner.os Tex.GitHub.Vars["REGION"] // vars.REGION Tex.GitHub.Event["label"]["name"] // github.event.label.name (JsonExpr) Tex.DevOps covers the common Azure DevOps predefined variables (Tex.DevOps.Build.SourceBranch, Tex.DevOps.System.AccessToken, Tex.DevOps.Agent.Os, …) and runtime expressions; see Azure DevOps Pipelines. Anything the catalogue doesn't cover can be reached through a JsonExpr indexer. Call AsString(), AsBool() or AsNumber() when you need to compare the result: Tex.GitHub.Event["label"]["name"].AsString().Eq("release") // github.event.label.name == 'release' Tex.GitHub.Event["label"]["name"].AsString().In(Tex.FromJson(Tex.Variable("RELEASE_LABELS"))) // contains(fromJSON(vars.RELEASE_LABELS), github.event.label.name) Functions Tex.Format("{0}-nuget-{1}", Tex.GitHub.Runner.Os, Tex.HashFiles("**/*.csproj")) // ${{ format('{0}-nuget-{1}', runner.os, hashFiles('**/*.csproj')) }} Tex.GitHub.Event.ToJson() // ${{ toJSON(github.event) }} Tex.GitHub.Ref.EndsWith("-rc") // endsWith(github.ref, '-rc') Interpolated templates cover most uses of format, so reach for Tex.Format only when the platform has to do the formatting at run time. The escape hatch: Tex.Raw Tex.Raw(text) inserts expression text verbatim. It is a BoolExpr that converts implicitly to the other expression types, so it works anywhere. When you combine it with other expressions it is parenthesized as a unit, so the result keeps its meaning: !Tex.Raw("github.ref == 'main'") // !(github.ref == 'main') Tex.Raw("github.event.forced") && Tex.Success() // github.event.forced && success() Prefer the typed members where they exist: raw text isn't checked, escaped or translated between platforms. Behavioral notes Conditions starting with !. A YAML value can't start with ! (it is a tag), so the GitHub writer wraps such a condition in ${{ }}: if: ${{ !contains(github.ref, '-') }}. Literals are quoted and escaped. Tex.GitHub.Ref.Eq("it's") prints github.ref == 'it''s'. Expressions are records. They compare structurally, and DescendantsAndSelf() walks the tree, which is how tools find the jobs a condition depends on (look for JobOutputRef nodes). ToString() is for debugging. It prints a neutral form; use the platform printer to get real output. Unsupported nodes fail loudly. A printer throws NotSupportedException for a node it can't express, such as Tex.FromJson in Azure DevOps. Printing expressions yourself The writers print expressions for you. To print one directly, for a test or a custom writer, use the platform's printer: GithubExpressionPrinter.Instance.Print(expression); // the bare expression GithubExpressionPrinter.Instance.Render(template); // a template, with ${{ }} around expressions GithubExpressionPrinter.Instance.PrintCondition(condition); // an if: value, wrapped only when it must be DevopsExpressionPrinter.Instance.Render(template); To target another platform, derive from ExpressionPrinter. The base class handles precedence, literal quoting, member access, casts and raw text. You implement WrapEmbedded (the template delimiters), PrintReference (how Tex.Secret, Tex.JobOutput and the other references are spelled) and PrintResult, and override the virtual members such as FunctionName or PrintLogical where the syntax differs. See also GitHub Actions Workflows: expressions in workflow models Azure DevOps Pipelines: Azure DevOps expression syntax Samples: runnable examples with their output Tex, Expr, Template, ExpressionPrinter

docs/faq.html.title: FAQ | Invex.StructuredText
docs/faq.html.summary: FAQ Answers to common questions about what the library does, how to use the models and expressions, and how to fix frequent problems. Check here when something behaves differently from what you expected. General What does this library actually do? It turns strongly-typed C# object graphs into YAML text for GitHub Actions workflows, Dependabot configs, and Azure DevOps Pipelines. You build models, a writer renders them, and you save the resulting string to a file. Does it parse existing YAML files? No. The library is write-only by design — it generates YAML from C# models. If you have existing hand-written workflows, port them to the model once and generate from then on. Does it run my pipelines? No. It only produces the configuration files. GitHub/Azure DevOps execute them as usual once committed. Which platforms and frameworks are supported? .NET 10.0. Generators are typically run as small console apps on any OS. Usage Why are some properties required and nullable at the same time? Model records deliberately force you to make a decision for schema-significant properties (e.g. On.Push.Branches). required ... { get; init; } with a nullable type means "you must say something, even if that something is null". This keeps generated YAML intentional rather than accidentally omitting filters. Where do I start when writing an expression? Type Tex.. Every way to create an expression is a member of that one class: references such as Tex.Secret and Tex.JobOutput, status checks such as Tex.Success(), functions, and the platform contexts Tex.GitHub and Tex.DevOps. Add using static Invex.StructuredText.Expressions.Tex; to drop the prefix. See Expressions. How do I write ${{ ... }} into a value? Put the expression in the value, on its own or in an interpolated string. The writer adds the delimiters: Env = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["SHA"] = Tex.GitHub.Sha, // ${{ github.sha }} ["TAG"] = $"v{Tex.JobOutput("setup", "version")}", // v${{ needs.setup.outputs.version }} }; Condition properties (If, Condition) are written without delimiters, as the platforms expect. How do I compare against a string? Pass a C# string: Tex.GitHub.EventName.Eq("push") prints github.event_name == 'push'. Literals are always quoted and escaped, so there is no separate "string" variant of each comparison. What if the API doesn't cover something? Index into a context (Tex.GitHub.Event["label"]["name"]), then call AsString(), AsBool() or AsNumber() to compare it. For anything else, Tex.Raw("...") inserts expression text verbatim and works wherever an expression is expected. Can I reuse one writer for several files? Writers accumulate output. Either create a fresh writer per file or call writer.TextWriter.Reset() between documents. How do I share common steps/jobs between workflows? That's the main payoff of generating from C#: use ordinary functions, constants, and composition. static Step CheckoutStep() => new Step.UsesStep { Uses = "actions/checkout@v6" }; static Job WithDefaults(Job job) => job with { TimeoutMinutes = 30 }; The union types — how do I pick a variant? Construct the nested record: new On.Push { ... }, new Step.RunStep { ... }, new DevopsPipeline.DevopsPipelineWithStages { ... }, new Pool.PoolSpec { ... }. The base type (On, Step, …) is what model properties accept. Is the output deterministic? Yes — same model, same text. That makes generated files diff-friendly, and lets you verify in CI that committed workflow files match the generator (regenerate and git diff --exit-code). Troubleshooting NotSupportedException when writing a model The platform printer met an expression it can't express, such as Tex.FromJson in Azure DevOps (which has no fromJSON), Tex.DevOps.Runtime(...) in a GitHub workflow, or a custom Expr subclass. Use an expression the target supports, or Tex.Raw with the platform's own syntax. My interpolated value lost its ${{ }} A conditional like isNightly ? $"Nightly {Tex.GitHub.RunNumber}" : "Release" has the type string, so C# formats the expression as plain text before the writer sees it. Cast the interpolated branch: isNightly ? (Template)$"Nightly {Tex.GitHub.RunNumber}" : "Release". My condition is wrapped in ${{ }} but the others aren't That's intended. A YAML value can't start with !, so the GitHub writer wraps conditions that start with a negation: if: ${{ !contains(github.ref, '-') }}. Where is the API reference? See the API Reference, generated from the XML documentation comments in the source. See also Expressions: Tex, conditions, templates and the Tex.Raw escape hatch Getting Started: the build, write, save pattern Architecture: why the models are shaped the way they are Tex, ExpressionPrinter

docs/getting-started.html.title: Getting Started | Invex.StructuredText
docs/getting-started.html.summary: Getting Started This page shows how to install the packages and generate your first GitHub Actions workflow, Azure DevOps pipeline, and Dependabot config. Start here if you have not used the library before. Requirements .NET 10.0 Installation Install the package for the platform you want to target. Each platform package automatically brings in the Invex.StructuredText core library. # GitHub Actions workflows + Dependabot configs dotnet add package Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions # Azure DevOps Pipelines dotnet add package Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines # Just the core writer and expression API dotnet add package Invex.StructuredText The general pattern Every generator in this library follows the same three-step pattern: Build a model — construct an object graph (GithubAction, DependabotConfig, or DevopsPipeline) using records with init properties and collection expressions. Write it — pass the model to the corresponding writer (GithubActionWriter, DependabotConfigWriter, or DevopsPipelineWriter). Get the text — call writer.TextWriter.ToString() and save it wherever you need. var writer = new GithubActionWriter(); writer.Write(myWorkflow); var yaml = writer.TextWriter.ToString(); File.WriteAllText(".github/workflows/ci.yml", yaml); Your first GitHub Actions workflow using Invex.StructuredText.Expressions; using Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions; using Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions.GithubActionModel; var workflow = new GithubAction { Name = "CI", On = [ new On.Push { Branches = ["main"], BranchesIgnore = null, Tags = null, TagsIgnore = null, Paths = null, PathsIgnore = null, }, ], Jobs = [ new Job { Name = "build", RunsOn = new() { Labels = ["ubuntu-latest"] }, Steps = [ new Step.UsesStep { Name = "Checkout", Uses = "actions/checkout@v6" }, new Step.RunStep { Name = "Build", If = Tex.GitHub.EventName.Eq("push"), Run = [$"dotnet build -c Release -p:Version=1.0.{Tex.GitHub.RunNumber}"], }, ], }, ], }; var writer = new GithubActionWriter(); writer.Write(workflow); Console.WriteLine(writer.TextWriter.ToString()); Output: name: CI on: push: branches: [ main ] jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - name: Checkout uses: actions/checkout@v6 - name: Build if: github.event_name == 'push' run: 'dotnet build -c Release -p:Version=1.0.${{ github.run_number }}' Plain strings are written as they are. Tex.GitHub.EventName.Eq("push") is a typed condition, and the interpolated Run line embeds github.run_number as an expression. Everything that creates an expression starts with Tex., so IntelliSense on Tex. is the quickest way to find what you need. See Expressions. Your first Azure DevOps pipeline using Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines; using Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines.DevopsPipelineModel.Pipeline; using Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines.DevopsPipelineModel.Steps; using Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines.DevopsPipelineModel.Triggers; using Invex.StructuredText.Expressions; var pipeline = new DevopsPipeline.DevopsPipelineWithSteps { Trigger = new Trigger.BranchList { Branches = ["main"] }, Steps = [ new Step.Script { ScriptContent = $"echo Building {Tex.DevOps.Build.SourceBranchName}", DisplayName = "Say hello", }, ], }; var writer = new DevopsPipelineWriter(); writer.Write(pipeline); Console.WriteLine(writer.TextWriter.ToString()); Output: trigger: branches: include: [ main ] steps: - script: echo Building $(Build.SourceBranchName) displayName: Say hello Your first Dependabot config using Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions; using Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions.DependabotConfigModel.Model; var config = new DependabotConfig { Updates = [ new DependabotUpdate { PackageEcosystem = "nuget", Directory = "/", Schedule = new() { Interval = ScheduleInterval.Weekly }, }, ], }; var writer = new DependabotConfigWriter(); writer.WriteConfig(config); File.WriteAllText(".github/dependabot.yml", writer.TextWriter.ToString()); A common workflow: generate-and-commit A typical setup is a small console project in your repository (e.g. _build/ or _atom/) that regenerates all workflow files. Run it locally or in CI, then commit the output. Because generation is deterministic, the diff shows exactly what changed. // Program.cs in a build-tool project var writer = new GithubActionWriter(); writer.Write(BuildCiWorkflow()); File.WriteAllText("../.github/workflows/ci.yml", writer.TextWriter.ToString()); writer = new GithubActionWriter(); // fresh writer per file writer.Write(BuildReleaseWorkflow()); File.WriteAllText("../.github/workflows/release.yml", writer.TextWriter.ToString()); Note Writers accumulate text in an internal StructuredTextWriter. Use a fresh writer per output file, or call writer.TextWriter.Reset() between writes. Next steps Expressions: conditions, references and interpolated values GitHub Actions Workflows: the full workflow model Azure DevOps Pipelines: stages, jobs, deployment strategies, resources Dependabot Configuration: registries, groups, schedules FAQ: common questions and troubleshooting API: GithubActionWriter, DependabotConfigWriter, DevopsPipelineWriter

docs/github-actions.html.title: GitHub Actions Workflows | Invex.StructuredText
docs/github-actions.html.summary: GitHub Actions Workflows The Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions package generates GitHub Actions workflow YAML from a strongly-typed model rooted at GithubAction (namespace Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions.GithubActionModel). Read this page when you want to go beyond the first example: triggers, jobs, steps, matrices, permissions, and passing outputs between jobs. var writer = new GithubActionWriter(); writer.Write(workflow); var yaml = writer.TextWriter.ToString(); The model at a glance GithubAction ├── Name, RunName ├── On (list of trigger events — discriminated union) ├── Permissions (All | Exact) ├── Env (dictionary of expressions) ├── Concurrency └── Jobs ├── Name, Needs, If, RunsOn, Environment, Concurrency ├── Permissions, Outputs, Env, TimeoutMinutes, ContinueOnError ├── Strategy (Matrix), Container, Services, Snapshot └── Steps (UsesStep | RunStep) Many model types are discriminated unions (generated with Dunet): you pick a variant by constructing the appropriate nested record, e.g. new On.Push { ... } or new Step.RunStep { ... }. Triggers (On) On is a union over all GitHub webhook events. Common variants: On = [ // Push to branches/tags/paths new On.Push { Branches = ["main"], BranchesIgnore = null, Tags = ["v*"], TagsIgnore = null, Paths = null, PathsIgnore = null, }, // Pull requests new On.PullRequest([On.PullRequest.PullRequestType.opened, On.PullRequest.PullRequestType.synchronize]) { Branches = ["main"], BranchesIgnore = null, Tags = null, TagsIgnore = null, Paths = null, PathsIgnore = null, }, // Cron schedules new On.Schedule(["0 6 * * 1"]), // Manual dispatch with typed inputs new On.WorkflowDispatch( [ new WorkflowDispatchInput.Boolean { Name = "dry-run", Description = "Skip publishing", Required = false, Default = "false", }, new WorkflowDispatchInput.Choice { Name = "configuration", Description = null, Required = true, Default = "Release", Options = ["Debug", "Release"], }, ]), // Reusable workflows / external triggers new On.WorkflowCall(), new On.RepositoryDispatch(["deploy"]), ] Other supported events include Release, IssueComment, Issues, Label, MergeGroup, Discussion, CheckRun, CheckSuite, WorkflowRun, Watch, Create, Delete, Fork, PageBuild, Public, Status, and more — each with its schema-accurate activity-type enum. Jobs new Job { Name = "test", RunsOn = new() { Labels = ["ubuntu-latest"] }, Needs = ["build"], // job dependencies If = Tex.GitHub.EventName.Eq("push"), TimeoutMinutes = 30, Env = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["DOTNET_NOLOGO"] = "true", }, Outputs = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["version"] = Tex.StepOutput("gitversion", "semVer"), }, Steps = [ /* ... */ ], } Name, TimeoutMinutes, Env and Outputs values are templates, so they accept plain text, a number, an expression or an interpolated string. If is a BoolExpr condition. See Expressions. Matrix strategies Strategy = new Strategy { Matrix = new Matrix { Map = new Dictionary<string, IReadOnlyList<Template>> { ["os"] = ["ubuntu-latest", "windows-latest", "macos-latest"], ["configuration"] = ["Debug", "Release"], }, Exclude = [ new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["os"] = "macos-latest", ["configuration"] = "Debug", }, ], }, FailFast = false, MaxParallel = 4, }, RunsOn = new() { Labels = [Tex.Matrix("os")] }, // ${{ matrix.os }} Permissions // Top-level or per-job: the same level for every scope (read-all / write-all) Permissions = new Permissions.All(PermissionsLevel.Read), // Or exact, per-scope Permissions = new Permissions.Exact(new PermissionsEvent { Contents = PermissionsLevel.Read, Packages = PermissionsLevel.Write, }), Concurrency, environments, containers Concurrency = new Concurrency { Group = $"ci-{Tex.GitHub.Ref}", // ci-${{ github.ref }} CancelInProgress = Tex.GitHub.EventName.Eq("pull_request"), }, Environment = new Environment { Name = "production" }, Container = new Container { Image = "mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0" }, Services = new Dictionary<string, Container> { ["postgres"] = new() { Image = "postgres:16" }, }, Steps Step is a union of two variants. Shared properties (Id, Name, If, Env, With, WorkingDirectory, ContinueOnError, TimeoutMinutes) live on the base record. UsesStep: run an action new Step.UsesStep { Name = "Setup .NET", Uses = "actions/setup-dotnet@v5", With = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["dotnet-version"] = "10.0.x", }, } RunStep: run shell commands Run is a list of templates; more than one entry produces a multi-line run: | block. new Step.RunStep { Id = "pack", Name = "Pack", Run = [ $"dotnet pack --configuration Release -p:Version={Tex.JobOutput("setup", "version")}", "dotnet nuget push *.nupkg --api-key \"$NUGET_API_KEY\"", ], Shell = "bash", Env = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["NUGET_API_KEY"] = Tex.Secret("NUGET_API_KEY"), // ${{ secrets.NUGET_API_KEY }} }, } Tip Pass secrets to commands through Env rather than interpolating them into Run, so they never appear in the generated script text. Conditional steps new Step.RunStep { Name = "Publish (main only)", If = Tex.GitHub.Ref.Eq("refs/heads/main") && Tex.Success(), Run = ["dotnet nuget push *.nupkg"], } This renders if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && success(). Conditions are written without ${{ }} unless they start with !, which YAML would read as a tag. Referencing outputs between steps and jobs A step output is published as a job output, and a later job reads it with Tex.JobOutput: new Job { Name = "build", RunsOn = new() { Labels = ["ubuntu-latest"] }, Outputs = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["version"] = Tex.StepOutput("gitversion", "semVer"), // ${{ steps.gitversion.outputs.semVer }} }, Steps = [ /* a step with Id = "gitversion" that writes semVer to $GITHUB_OUTPUT */ ], }, new Job { Name = "release", Needs = ["build"], If = !Tex.JobOutput("build", "version").Contains("-"), // stable versions only RunsOn = new() { Labels = ["ubuntu-latest"] }, Env = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["VERSION"] = Tex.JobOutput("build", "version"), // ${{ needs.build.outputs.version }} }, Steps = [ /* ... */ ], } The release job's condition becomes if: ${{ !contains(needs.build.outputs.version, '-') }}. Complete example var workflow = new GithubAction { Name = "CI", On = [ new On.Push { Branches = ["main"], BranchesIgnore = null, Tags = null, TagsIgnore = null, Paths = null, PathsIgnore = null, }, ], Permissions = new Permissions.Exact(new PermissionsEvent { Contents = PermissionsLevel.Read, }), Concurrency = new Concurrency { Group = $"ci-{Tex.GitHub.Ref}", CancelInProgress = true, }, Jobs = [ new Job { Name = "build", RunsOn = new() { Labels = ["ubuntu-latest"] }, Steps = [ new Step.UsesStep { Uses = "actions/checkout@v6" }, new Step.UsesStep { Uses = "actions/setup-dotnet@v5", With = new Dictionary<string, Template> { ["dotnet-version"] = "10.0.x" }, }, new Step.RunStep { Run = ["dotnet build -c Release"] }, new Step.RunStep { Run = ["dotnet test -c Release --no-build"] }, ], }, ], }; var writer = new GithubActionWriter(); writer.Write(workflow); File.WriteAllText(".github/workflows/ci.yml", writer.TextWriter.ToString()); The samples include a larger workflow with a version job, a test matrix, a stable-only publish job and failure reporting, together with its output. See also Expressions: the expression system used throughout the model Dependabot Configuration: generating dependabot.yml with the same package StructuredTextWriter: the writer behind GithubActionWriter.TextWriter GithubAction, GithubActionWriter, GithubExpressionPrinter

docs/introduction.html.title: Introduction | Invex.StructuredText
docs/introduction.html.summary: Introduction Invex.StructuredText is a family of strongly-typed C# libraries for generating structured YAML text files — specifically GitHub Actions workflows, Dependabot configurations, and Azure DevOps Pipelines. This page explains why you would generate CI/CD YAML from C#, when the library is (and is not) a good fit, and the concepts the rest of the documentation builds on. Why generate YAML from C#? CI/CD configuration files grow quickly. Hand-written YAML suffers from: No compile-time validation — typos in keys, indentation mistakes, and invalid values are only discovered when the pipeline runs (or fails to parse). No refactoring support — renaming a job, output, or variable means find-and-replace across files and hoping you caught every reference. Duplication — YAML has limited reuse mechanisms, so common patterns get copy-pasted between workflows. Stringly-typed expressions — ${{ }} and $( ) expressions are opaque strings to your editor. Invex.StructuredText solves these problems by letting you define your pipelines as C# object graphs: Full IntelliSense and compile-time validation for every property Models closely follow the official schemas (GitHub workflow schema, Dependabot v2 schema, Azure Pipelines YAML schema) Typed expressions written with C# operators and interpolated strings, printed as GitHub's ${{ }} syntax or Azure DevOps macro, template and runtime syntax Deterministic, cleanly formatted YAML output that is easy to diff and review When to use it Invex.StructuredText is a good fit when: You maintain several workflows or pipelines that share jobs, steps, or conventions, and want to reuse them with ordinary C# functions and constants. You maintain many repositories and want their CI configuration generated from one shared definition. You already have a C# build tool (for example an _atom/ or _build/ console project) that can regenerate the files and check them in. Expressions are getting complicated, and you want conditions and output references checked by the compiler instead of discovered at run time. It is not the right tool when: You need to read or modify existing YAML. The library is write-only; it does not parse workflow files. You have one small workflow. Writing the YAML by hand is simpler than adding a generator project. You target another CI system. Only GitHub Actions, Dependabot, and Azure DevOps Pipelines have models, although the core writer and expression system can be used to build your own (see Architecture). Key concepts at a glance Concept What it is Model An object graph of records rooted at GithubAction, DependabotConfig, or DevopsPipeline. Union variant Schema "one of" shapes (a step is run: or uses:) are discriminated unions; construct the nested variant you need, such as new Step.RunStep { ... }. Writer GithubActionWriter, DependabotConfigWriter, or DevopsPipelineWriter walks a model and emits YAML. StructuredTextWriter The indentation-aware buffer every writer writes into; read the result with writer.TextWriter.ToString(). See StructuredTextWriter. Tex The single entry point for expressions: Tex holds references (Tex.Secret, Tex.JobOutput, …), status checks, functions, and the platform contexts Tex.GitHub and Tex.DevOps. See Expressions. Expression A typed tree (BoolExpr, StringExpr, NumberExpr, JsonExpr) that a platform printer writes in that platform's syntax. Conditions are BoolExpr. Template Text with expressions embedded in it. Every other expression-capable property is a Template, created from a string or an interpolated string. Design principles Model the schema, not a DSL. Model records mirror the official YAML schemas and their property names map mechanically to YAML keys, so platform documentation applies directly. Invalid shapes do not compile. Discriminated unions rule out combinations the schema forbids, and required properties force a decision on schema-significant values, even when that decision is null. Write once, render per platform. Expressions are platform-agnostic trees; only the printer knows the target syntax. Typed where it matters. Conditions must be BoolExpr, and each expression type offers only the operations that make sense for it, so mistakes show up as compile errors. Deterministic and write-only. The same model always produces the same text, so you can regenerate in CI and fail on git diff --exit-code. Small, composable layers. Platform packages are built on a core writer and expression system that you can reuse for your own generators. The packages Package What it provides Invex.StructuredText The core: StructuredTextWriter (indentation-aware text writer) and the expression API (Tex) Invex.StructuredText.GithubActions GithubActionWriter, DependabotConfigWriter, GithubExpressionPrinter, Tex.GitHub, and model types Invex.StructuredText.AzureDevopsPipelines DevopsPipelineWriter, DevopsExpressionPrinter, Tex.DevOps, and model types Both platform packages depend on the core package, so installing either one gives you everything you need. Next steps Getting Started — install the packages and generate your first file Expressions — conditions, references and interpolated values GitHub Actions Workflows — workflow generation in depth Dependabot Configuration — dependabot.yml generation Azure DevOps Pipelines — pipeline generation in depth Architecture — how the pieces fit together

docs/structured-text-writer.html.title: StructuredTextWriter | Invex.StructuredText
docs/structured-text-writer.html.summary: StructuredTextWriter StructuredTextWriter (in the Invex.StructuredText namespace) is the low-level, indentation-aware text writer that all the YAML generators are built on. You only need it directly if you are writing your own generator or extending an existing one — but understanding it helps explain how the higher-level writers produce their output. Basics using Invex.StructuredText; var writer = new StructuredTextWriter(); // default indent size: 2 spaces writer.WriteLine("name: CI"); writer.WriteLine(); Console.WriteLine(writer.ToString()); Member Description Write(text, indent = true) Appends text without a newline; optionally skips the indent prefix WriteLine(text = null) Appends a line at the current indent level (or a blank line) WriteSection(text = null) Optionally writes a header line, then increases the indent; returns an IDisposable that restores it Reset(indentSize = 2) Clears the buffer and resets indentation Indent / IndentSize Current indent level and the number of spaces per level StringBuilder The underlying buffer ToString() Returns the accumulated text Sections and scoped indentation WriteSection is the heart of the API. It writes an (optional) header line and bumps the indent level. Disposing the returned scope restores the previous level, so nesting maps naturally onto C# using blocks: var writer = new StructuredTextWriter(); using (writer.WriteSection("jobs:")) { using (writer.WriteSection("build:")) { writer.WriteLine("runs-on: ubuntu-latest"); using (writer.WriteSection("steps:")) { writer.WriteLine("- run: dotnet build"); } } } Console.WriteLine(writer.ToString()); jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: dotnet build Reset and versioning Reset() clears the buffer, resets the indent, and increments an internal Version. Any section scopes that were created before the reset become no-ops on dispose — they will not corrupt the indentation of content written after the reset. This makes it safe to reuse a single writer across multiple documents: var writer = new StructuredTextWriter(); // ... write first document ... var first = writer.ToString(); writer.Reset(); // ... write second document ... var second = writer.ToString(); Using it with the high-level writers Each platform writer exposes its StructuredTextWriter via the TextWriter property: var actionWriter = new GithubActionWriter(); actionWriter.Write(workflow); var yaml = actionWriter.TextWriter.ToString(); You can also supply your own instance (for example, to share one buffer or use a different indent size): var writer = new GithubActionWriter { TextWriter = new StructuredTextWriter(indentSize: 4), }; See also Architecture: how the writers and formatters fit together Getting Started: reusing writers across files StructuredTextWriter
